levels.title: First sounds
levels.subtitle: Open strings, your first chord and your first change.

lessons.title: Meet the six strings
theory: Strings are numbered from the thinnest (1st, high E) to the thickest (6th, low E).
Open, from low to high: E – A – D – G – B – E.
Tune before every session: an out-of-tune guitar makes even good playing sound wrong.
Before you play, check the basics: sit up, the guitar's waist on your leg, the neck tilted slightly up. A relaxed body plays cleaner and longer.
tips: Rest the pick on the string and let it go: a firm attack without brushing the neighbors.
If an open string buzzes, check the tuning and make sure your other hand isn't touching it.
tutorials: how to tune a guitar for beginners

exercises.title: Play the 6 open strings, from the 6th to the 1st
exercises.theory: The open strings, low to high, spell E A D G B E. Each one is a fourth above the last, except G to B, which is a major third: that's why one string "breaks" every pattern on the guitar.

exercises.title: And back, from the 1st to the 6th
exercises.theory: Going down from the 1st to the 6th string, the pitch drops each time. Let each string ring until the next one sounds: that's the first step toward a clean, connected sound.

lessons.title: Parts of the guitar and reading tab
theory: The headstock holds the tuners, the neck holds the frets, and the body holds the bridge (and, on an electric, the pickups).
Frets are counted from the nut: fret 1 is the one closest to the headstock. In tab, 0 means the open string.
Tab draws the six strings as six lines and a number on a line tells you which fret to press. Each line starts with its string's name (E A D G B e), so you always know which is which.

Here the 6th string (low E) is on the top line, like the guitar as you look down at it. Most printed tab puts the 1st string (high e) on top instead: you can switch to that in Settings → Instrument, and every tab and fretboard follows.
Read tab from left to right, like text. Numbers stacked in the same column are played together.
tips: Say the string and the fret out loud before you play each number: it makes reading automatic sooner.
tutorials: how to read guitar tab for beginners

exercises.title: Strings and tab
exercises.theory: Tab is a map of the neck, not of the music's rhythm: lines are strings, numbers are frets. Knowing which line is which string is half of reading it.

exercises.title: Play what the tab says
exercises.theory: This tab climbs string by string: open, then a fretted note on the same string. Read one column at a time and say the string and fret before you play it.

lessons.title: One finger per fret
theory: One finger per fret: in a four-fret span, finger 1 plays the first fret, finger 2 the second, and so on. The hand stays still and the fingers do the walking.
Press with the fingertip right behind the fret, not on top of it. Behind is clean; too far back buzzes; on top sounds muted.
Press first, then pick: if the pick gets there before the finger is down, the note buzzes.
Slow and even beats fast and messy. This chromatic walk is the classic warm-up: it wakes up both hands and teaches them to work together.

exercises.title: 1-2-3-4 up four strings
exercises.theory: Each fret is a half step, so this walk plays every note in order: the chromatic scale. It's not about music yet; it's about each finger owning its fret.

exercises.title: 4-3-2-1 back down
exercises.theory: Coming down, keep the lower fingers ready but relaxed, lifting each finger only as the next note sounds. That small overlap is what makes notes connect.

exercises.title: 1-3-2-4: finger independence
exercises.theory: Changing the finger order breaks the habit of moving fingers in a row. Fingers 3 and 4 share tendons, so they learn to move on their own slowly.

exercises.title: Buzzes and dead notes: causes and cures
exercises.theory: Most bad notes have a short list of causes: the finger's distance from the fret, a finger touching a neighbour string, or picking before pressing.

lessons.title: Your first chord: E minor
theory: A chord is several notes at once. Em uses only two fingers and all six strings ring.
Middle finger on fret 2 of the 5th string, ring finger on fret 2 of the 4th string.
Press with the fingertip, right behind the metal fret, with the thumb behind the neck.

If a note buzzes, the finger is too far from the fret or not pressing yet: slide it right behind the fret, and pick only once it's down. If a note sounds dead, a finger is lying on that string: arch the finger more.
tips: If a string sounds muted, a finger is touching it: arch your knuckles more.

exercises.title: Strum Em four times, clean
exercises.theory: Em is a minor triad (E, G, B) spread over six strings: the open strings already give you E, G and B, your two fingers add the B and E an octave up. Every string has to ring: if one is dead, a finger is touching it.

lessons.title: Am and your first change
theory: Am has the same shape as E, one string lower. Don't play the 6th string.
In the Em→Am change, the middle and ring fingers travel together one string toward the floor.
When a change won't come: play only the two chords, slowly, and practice just the move between them. Then put it back in the song.
tips: Practice the change slowly without strumming: look at the shape, then close your eyes.
tutorials: e minor to a minor chord change guitar

exercises.title: Strum Am four times
exercises.theory: Am is A, C and E. The open A string is the root, so start the strum on the 5th string: the low E would put the fifth in the bass and blur the chord.

exercises.title: Em → Am → Em → Am…
exercises.theory: Em and Am use the same two-finger shape, one string apart, and both contain the note E. Move the fingers as a block and watch where they land, not where they leave.

exercises.title: With the metronome at 70%
exercises.theory: Each chord lasts a whole bar of four beats. Change on beat 1: start moving during beat 4 of the previous bar so the new chord sounds right on the click.

levels.title: Open chords
levels.subtitle: The chords behind thousands of songs, and the color chords one finger away from them.

lessons.title: D, A and E
theory: A and E are the same shape moved one string: three fingers (A) versus two plus one (E).
Strum D from the 4th string: the two low strings stay silent.
tutorials: d a e chords guitar beginner

exercises.title: Strum D four times
exercises.theory: D is D, F# and A. Its root is the open 4th string, so the two lowest strings stay out. The 3rd (F#) is on top: press it well, it's what makes the chord major.

exercises.title: D ↔ A
exercises.theory: D and A are the I and V of D major: the V wants to go back to the I. Change without stopping the strumming hand; a late chord is better than a broken pulse.

exercises.title: Three major chords at 80%
exercises.theory: D, A and E are three major chords; in A major they're IV, I and V, the three chords of countless songs. Hear which one feels like home.

lessons.title: G and C
theory: G uses all six strings; C leaves the 6th out.
With G, C, D and Em you can already play pop's favorite progression: I–V–vi–IV.
tutorials: I V vi IV progression guitar

exercises.title: G ↔ C
exercises.theory: G and C are I and IV in G (or V and I in C). The open G string sounds in both chords: let it ring as a bridge between them.

exercises.title: Pop in G at 75%
exercises.theory: I–V–vi–IV in G is G–D–Em–C. Three of its four chords are major; the vi (Em) is the relative minor and gives the progression its bittersweet turn.

lessons.title: Color chords: one finger changes everything
theory: Many chords are a shape you already know with one finger added, lifted or moved: Dsus4 adds the pinky to D, Dsus2 lifts a finger off it, Em7 adds a finger to Em.
sus means suspended: the third (the note that makes a chord major or minor) is swapped for the 2nd or the 4th. It sounds open, waiting, and it usually goes back to the plain chord.
Fmaj7 is F without the barre: the same 3-2-1 fingers on the top four strings. Cadd9 is C with a high D on top.
tips: Keep the fingers that don't move pressed down: the anchor is what makes these changes fast.

exercises.title: D ↔ Dsus4
exercises.theory: Dsus4 replaces the 3rd (F#) with the 4th (G). The 4th sits a half step above the 3rd and wants to fall back: that's the classic sus4 → major release.

exercises.title: Folk in D with suspended chords
exercises.theory: Suspended chords decorate the plain ones without changing the harmony: the bass stays, only the top note moves. Keep the strum steady and let that one finger do the talking.

exercises.title: Anchor fingers: Em7, G, Dsus4, Cadd9
exercises.theory: Em7, G, Dsus4 and Cadd9 keep fingers 3 and 4 on the same frets of the top two strings. Those anchors stay down while the rest moves: fewer fingers to move, faster changes.

levels.title: Rhythm
levels.subtitle: Strumming, time signatures and the right hand.

lessons.title: Down and up
theory: The strumming hand swings like a pendulum, always in time, even when it misses the strings.
Down strums land on the numbers (1, 2, 3, 4) and up strums on the "ands".
The pattern D.DU.UDU is counted: 1, 2 and, and 4 and.
Practice slow first. Speed is a result: once a pattern is even and relaxed at a slow tempo, raise the metronome a few BPM at a time.
tutorials: basic strumming pattern guitar down up

exercises.title: Ballad in C with the metronome
exercises.theory: The pendulum never stops: the hand moves down on every number and up on every "and", and simply misses the strings on the rests. The pattern comes from which strokes touch the strings.

lessons.title: Three-four time
theory: In 3/4 you count ONE-two-three: the first beat is heavier.
E7 is E without the ring finger: the tension that resolves back to Am.
The first beat of each bar carries the accent. In 3/4 that gives the ONE-two-three sway of a waltz; in 4/4 the accent falls on 1 and, more lightly, on 3.

exercises.title: Waltz in A minor
exercises.theory: In 3/4 the bar has three beats and the first is the strong one: a bass-heavy strum on 1 and lighter strums on 2 and 3 make it sound like a waltz.

levels.title: Reading rhythm
levels.subtitle: Note values, rests and the pulse, tapped and then played.

lessons.title: The pulse
theory: The pulse is the steady beat you tap with your foot. BPM says how many beats fit in a minute: 60 BPM is one per second.
Most music counts in groups of four (4/4 time). The first beat of each group is the strongest, and the metronome marks it with a higher click.
Tap with the foot and play with the hands: the body keeps the pulse while the hands do the rest.
tips: Tap Space (or the pad) with each note. The first bar is only the count-in: listen before you play.
tutorials: how to count beats in music
captions: Four quarter notes: one note on every beat.

exercises.title: Tap the quarter notes
patterns: q q q q
q q q q
q q q q
q q q q
exercises.theory: The pulse is a grid of equal beats. Tapping with the click trains you to land exactly on it, not just near it.

lessons.title: What each note is worth
theory: Each note value says how long the note lasts. In 4/4 the quarter note is one beat, and the others are doubles and halves of it.
Whole note = 4 beats, half note = 2, quarter = 1, eighth = ½, sixteenth = ¼. Every value has a rest that lasts just as long.
tips: In tab, these same values often show up as stems under the fret numbers. Look for them next time you open a song.
tutorials: note values explained whole half quarter eighth

figures.pattern: e e e e e e e e

captions: A whole note: the whole bar.
Two half notes.
Four quarter notes.
Eight eighth notes: two per beat.

exercises.title: How long does it last?
exercises.theory: Note values are proportions: each one is half of the one before. Once you know the quarter note is one beat, every other value is a multiplication or a division.

lessons.title: Long notes
theory: With long notes you play once and keep counting while the note rings. The hard part is not rushing the next one.
Ties join two notes of the same pitch into one longer note: you play the first and keep counting through the second.
A dot after a note adds half its value: a dotted half lasts three beats, perfect for a full bar of 3/4.
captions: Two half notes: play on 1 and on 3.

exercises.title: Tap halves and wholes
patterns: h h
q q h
h q q
w
q h q
exercises.theory: A half note lasts two clicks and a whole note four. Count the beats out loud while the note lasts: the next attack must land on its own click, not before.

lessons.title: Eighth notes
theory: Eighth notes split each beat in two. Count "one-and, two-and": the note on the "and" falls right between two clicks.
When strumming eighths the hand goes down on the numbers and up on the "ands". Keep the hand moving even when a stroke is silent.
tips: A lot of rock rhythm guitar is steady eighths. Get them even and half the songs get easier.

figures.pattern: e e e e q q

captions: Eighths on beats 1 and 2, quarters on 3 and 4.

exercises.title: Tap the eighths
patterns: e e e e q q
q e e q e e
e e q e e q
q q e e e e
e e e e e e e e
exercises.theory: Two eighths fill one beat: the first lands on the click, the second exactly halfway to the next one. Say "one-and" to place it.

lessons.title: Rests
theory: A rest is time you count in silence. On the guitar, muting the strings at the right moment matters as much as playing.
Every value has a matching rest: whole, half, quarter, eighth and sixteenth. Same length, but in silence.
captions: Play, rest, play, rest.

exercises.title: Tap around the rests
patterns: q rq q rq
rq q rq q
q q rh
e e rq e e rq
rq e e q rq
exercises.theory: A rest has a length, just like a note. Keep counting through it; the note after a rest is where most people rush.

lessons.title: Mixing it all
theory: Now at 80 BPM. Read the whole bar during the count-in, before you start.
Count every beat, even the ones without a note. Most mistakes happen on a beat nobody played.

exercises.title: Values and rests together
patterns: q e e h
e e rq q q
h e e q
q re e q rq
e e e e h
rq q e e q
exercises.theory: Reading rhythm means grouping: see each beat as a block (one quarter, two eighths, a rest) instead of reading note by note.

lessons.title: Rhythm on the guitar
theory: Now swap the tap for the guitar: play the open low E string in the rhythm. guitarr hears every attack and its timing.
Timing is measured at the attack, the moment the pick hits. A clean attack on time matters more than a long sustain.
tips: Mute the string on the rests: if it keeps ringing, the next attack is harder to hear.
If your notes always come out late, measure the latency once with guitarr calibrate.

exercises.title: Play the bars on the low E
patterns: q q q q
e e e e q q
q rq q rq
h e e q
e e rq e e rq
exercises.theory: On the guitar a rest needs an action: lift the fretting fingers or touch the string with the picking hand so the note stops on time.

levels.title: Color
levels.subtitle: Blues, seventh chords and power chords.

lessons.title: Sevenths and the blues
theory: A seventh chord adds a note that wants to resolve: that's why the blues always feels in motion.
The 12-bar blues: I I I I · IV IV I I · V IV I V.

exercises.title: A7 ↔ D7
exercises.theory: A7 and D7 are the I7 and IV7 of a blues in A. In the blues even the I chord is a dominant 7: that tension that never fully resolves is the style's color.

exercises.title: Blues in A
exercises.theory: Twelve bars in three groups of four: I for four, IV for two and back to I, then V–IV–I and the turnaround. Count the bars and you never get lost.

lessons.title: Seventh chords
theory: A seventh chord is a triad plus one more note, the 7th. It adds color and, above all, direction: it wants to go somewhere.
Three families: dominant 7 (G7, C7) is tense and falls a fifth down; minor 7 (Am7, Dm7) is soft; major 7 (Cmaj7) is calm and dreamy.
Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7 is the ii–V–I: the most common chord move in jazz, and in a lot of pop too.
tips: Most open sevenths are a chord you know with one finger lifted or added: look for the shape you already have.
tutorials: ii V I guitar open chords

exercises.title: G7 → C
exercises.theory: G7 holds B and F, a tritone apart. B rises a half step to C and F falls a half step to E: that pull is why a dominant 7 resolves so strongly to its I.

exercises.title: ii–V–I in C
exercises.theory: Dm7 → G7 → Cmaj7: the roots move up a fourth each time, and the 7th of each chord falls by step to the 3rd of the next.

lessons.title: Power chords
theory: A power chord is root plus fifth: neither major nor minor, which is why it sounds great with distortion.
It's a movable shape: the same fingering on any fret.
With the root on the 6th string (E5, G5, F5) or on the 5th (A5, C5, B5, D5): learn where the notes are on those two strings and you can play any power chord.
Drop D tuning lowers the 6th string to D: power chords with the root on the 6th string become a single finger barring three strings, a staple of heavy riffs.

exercises.title: Power-chord rock
exercises.theory: A power chord has no 3rd, so distortion doesn't turn it into mud: the root and fifth produce a clean, strong combination even when the signal is clipped.

levels.title: Barre chords and melody
levels.subtitle: F with a barre, moving shapes, barre sevenths and your first scale.

lessons.title: F with a barre
theory: A barre is the index pressing every string on one fret: lay it on its side, not flat.
F is the E shape barred at fret 1. Move it and you get any major chord.
If the barre buzzes, check one string at a time and move the index closer to the fret. Most barres need less force than you think, but in the right place.
tips: Don't squeeze harder: pull your arm back and let its weight do the pressing.
tutorials: how to play f barre chord guitar

exercises.title: F four times, all six strings ringing
exercises.theory: F is the open E shape moved up one fret, with the index doing the job of the nut. Roll the index slightly onto its bony side and keep it close to the fret; pull with the arm's weight rather than squeezing with the thumb.

exercises.title: Andalusian cadence
exercises.theory: The Andalusian cadence walks down in minor: i–VII–VI–V (Am–G–F–E). The E at the end is major, borrowed from harmonic minor, and it pulls straight back to Am.

lessons.title: Moving barre chords
theory: A barre shape has no open strings, so it moves: slide it along the neck and the chord changes name, not fingering.
E shape (root on the 6th string): F at fret 1, F#m at fret 2 in its minor form, Gm at 3. A shape (root on the 5th string): Bb at fret 1, B and Bm at 2, C#m at 4.
To name a barre chord, find its root: the note under your index on the 6th or 5th string.
tips: Between two barres, ease the pressure while you move and squeeze again only when you land.
tutorials: e shape a shape barre chords

exercises.title: F ↔ Gm: the same hand two frets up
exercises.theory: F and Gm both use the E-shape barre, two frets apart. Only the middle finger changes: lift it and Gm's minor 3rd appears. Same hand, new chord.

exercises.title: Moving barre chords
exercises.theory: Name each barre by the note under the index on the 6th or 5th string. If you know the notes on those two strings, you can play any major or minor chord.

lessons.title: Barre sevenths
theory: The sevenths you know in open position also move: F7 is the E7 shape with a barre, Bb7 the A7 shape, Bm7 the Am7 shape and F#m7 the Em7 shape.
With these four shapes you can play a dominant 7 and a minor 7 with the root on the 6th or 5th string, in any key: the basis of blues in any key and of jazz comping.
tips: Lift a finger from a barre chord you know and see which seventh appears: the barre stays where it was.
tutorials: barre seventh chords guitar e shape a shape

exercises.title: F7 ↔ Bb7
exercises.theory: F7 to Bb7 is I7 to IV7 of a blues in F. The two shapes sit at the same fret, root on the 6th string and then on the 5th: one jump across strings, no slide.

exercises.title: Bm7 ↔ F#m7
exercises.theory: Bm7 and F#m7 are minor 7 chords a fourth apart. A minor 7 is a minor triad plus a flat 7: softer than a dominant, and very common in pop and soul.

lessons.title: A minor pentatonic
theory: The pentatonic scale has 5 notes: most rock and blues solos are improvised with it.
Position 1 at fret 5: index on 5, ring or pinky on 7/8.
Practice scales slowly and evenly with a metronome, saying the root each time you pass it. Speed comes after the fingering is automatic.
tutorials: a minor pentatonic scale guitar position 1

exercises.title: Climb the scale, note by note
exercises.theory: A minor pentatonic is A C D E G: the minor scale without its 2nd and 6th. With no half steps, almost any note sounds fine over a minor or blues backing.

exercises.title: And come back down
exercises.theory: Coming down, lead with the same fingering: two notes per string, index on fret 5. Say the root (A) out loud each time you pass it: it's your home base.

levels.title: Guitar technique
levels.subtitle: Alternate and economy picking, palm mute, legato, bends and vibrato.

lessons.title: Alternate picking
theory: With alternate picking every note switches the pick direction: down (⊓) and up (V). In sixteenths the rule is simple: on the beat and on the "and" the pick goes down; on the "e" and the "a" (the inner sixteenths) it goes up.
Hold the pick between the thumb and the side of the index finger, with little tip showing. The motion is small and comes from the wrist, like shaking off a drop of water.
tips: When there's a rest, keep the hand moving up and down in the air: that way the direction of the next note is never lost.

figures.pattern: s s s s s s s s q q

captions: Sixteenths: ⊓ V ⊓ V ⊓ V ⊓ V.

exercises.title: Alternate picking on the low E
patterns: s s s s s s s s q q
e e s s s s e e s s s s
q s s s s q s s s s
s s s s q s s s s q
exercises.theory: Down on the beats and the "ands", up on the "e" and "a". If the hand always moves in time, the direction of each note is decided by the rhythm, never by guessing.

exercises.title: How the picking hand works
exercises.theory: Picking is a small, relaxed wrist motion. Tension is the enemy of speed: the less you squeeze the pick, the faster and more even you can play.

lessons.title: Palm mute
theory: In palm muting (P.M.) the side of the picking hand rests lightly on the strings, right over the bridge. The note comes out short and low, with that chug. Too far forward and the note disappears; too far back and nothing is muted.
The contrast between muted and open notes is what gives a riff its weight: the open ones come out as accents.
tips: Use downstrokes on the muted eighths: the sound gets firmer and more even.

figures.pattern: e e e e e e q

captions: Muted eighths (PM) and an open quarter at the end.

exercises.title: Chug on the low E
patterns: e e e e e e q
e e q e e q
s s e s s e e e q
e e re e e e re e
exercises.theory: Rest the edge of the picking hand right where the strings leave the bridge. Move it a few millimeters toward the neck for more mute, toward the bridge for more tone.

lessons.title: Economy picking and string skipping
theory: Economy picking: when you change strings in the same direction as the stroke, the pick goes straight on to the next string instead of coming back. Moving down from the 5th string to the 4th, the last note on the 5th and the first on the 4th are both downstrokes, in one motion.
String skipping means jumping over a string (or more) between notes. It takes aim with the pick and muting: the skipped string must not ring.
tips: With strict alternate picking the hand never changes its pattern; with economy picking it slides. Both work; what matters is knowing which one you're using.

exercises.title: Octaves, skipping a string
exercises.theory: Octaves two strings apart: two strings up and two frets up (three frets once you cross the B string). The string in between must stay silent: let the fretting finger touch it lightly.

exercises.title: Economy, alternate and skipping
exercises.theory: Economy picking saves motion on string changes; alternate picking keeps the rhythm locked. Most players mix both depending on the line.

lessons.title: Fingerstyle: p, i, m, a
theory: In fingerstyle the picking-hand fingers have names from Spanish: p (pulgar, thumb), i (índice), m (medio), a (anular). The thumb plays the bass strings (6, 5, 4); i, m and a usually take strings 3, 2 and 1.
In an arpeggio the fretting hand holds a chord while the picking hand plays its notes one by one, never using the same finger twice in a row.
Rest the wrist relaxed above the strings and move from the knuckles. Keep every note the same volume: listen to the thumb against the fingers.
Where you pluck changes the tone: near the bridge it's bright and crisp; over the end of the neck it's round and sweet. Electric players use the pickup switch for the same thing.

exercises.title: C: p i m a m i
exercises.theory: The thumb plays the root on the 5th string, then i-m-a climb the top three strings and come back. Hold the whole C chord so every note keeps ringing.

exercises.title: Am: the same pattern
exercises.theory: Same right-hand pattern, new chord: in fingerstyle the pattern stays and the chords change underneath it.

exercises.title: G: thumb on the 6th string
exercises.theory: When the root is on the 6th string, the thumb moves there. The thumb follows the bass note; the fingers stay on their strings.

lessons.title: Legato
theory: Legato means playing several notes with a single pick stroke and doing the rest with the fretting hand: hammer-on (h) to go up, pull-off (p) to come down. The sound flows, like a voice singing.

Hammer-on: bring the finger down firmly, right behind the fret. Pull-off: as you leave, pull the string slightly sideways (toward the floor). The slurred notes have to sound as loud as the picked one.
tips: Mute the neighboring strings: with legato any loose string touching ringing along gets in.
tutorials: hammer on pull off legato exercises guitar

figures.pattern: te te te q te te te q

captions: Triplets: pick only the first of each group, slur the other two.

exercises.title: Hammer and pull in A minor pentatonic
exercises.theory: One pick stroke per string, then the fretting hand does the rest: hammer up, pull back down. Aim for three notes of equal volume.

exercises.title: Clean legato
exercises.theory: In legato the other strings tend to ring when you pull off. Mute them with the fretting fingers and the side of the picking hand.

lessons.title: Finger workouts
theory: Finger exercises train what songs take for granted: each finger landing on its fret, on time, with the others relaxed.
Keep the fingers close to the strings. A finger that flies two centimeters away takes longer to come back: small, efficient motions are what speed is made of.
Leave fingers down when you can: in an ascending run, finger 1 can stay pressed while 2, 3 and 4 play. Lift them one by one as you come back down.
Permutations (1-3-2-4, 4-2-3-1…) break the habit of always moving fingers in the same order, which is where clumsiness hides. Five minutes a day, slow and with a metronome, beats an hour once a week.

exercises.title: The spider: fingers in pairs across strings
exercises.theory: Fingers 1 and 2 play on two neighbouring strings, then 3 and 4 do the same. Each finger stays down until its partner plays: that independence is the whole point.

exercises.title: Permutation 4-2-3-1 at fret 5
exercises.theory: Starting with the pinky and jumping between fingers trains the weakest finger first. Keep the hand still in 5th position: only the fingers move.

exercises.title: 1-3-4 on every string
exercises.theory: 1-3-4 (a whole step, then a half step) is one of the two finger groups of almost every major-scale fingering. The ring and pinky work as a team.

exercises.title: 1-2-4 on every string
exercises.theory: 1-2-4 (a half step, then a whole step) is the other group. With 1-3-4 and 1-2-4 you can play any major or minor scale in one position.

exercises.title: Trills: 1-2, 1-3 and 1-4
exercises.theory: A trill alternates two notes with hammer-ons and pull-offs. Finger 1 stays down the whole time; the upper finger does all the work. Every note should sound equally loud.

exercises.title: Shifting chromatic: one fret up on every string
exercises.theory: The hand moves up one fret each time it changes string. Shift on the last note of the string, sliding the whole hand, so the next string starts already in place.

lessons.title: Bends and vibrato
theory: A bend pushes (or pulls) the string sideways until the note goes up. A whole-step bend has to land exactly on the note two frets up; a half-step bend, on the note one fret up. Test it: play the target note fretted, then bend and compare.
Use more than one finger: finger 3 pushes while fingers 1 and 2 help behind it on the same string. The strength comes from turning the wrist, not from the fingers.
Vibrato is a small bend repeated: up and back to the note, in a steady rhythm. Wide and slow or narrow and fast, it's every guitarist's signature.
tips: Let the listener be the judge: it only counts the bend once it reaches the target pitch.

exercises.title: Bends in tune
exercises.theory: Bending is tuning while you play: the target pitch is fixed, your ear checks it. A bend that stops short sounds out of tune, not expressive.

exercises.title: Half-step bend: B string, fret 10 → B♭
exercises.theory: A half-step bend raises the note by one fret's worth. Play fret 11 first to hear the target, then bend fret 10 until it matches.

levels.title: Fingerpicking and arpeggios
levels.subtitle: Picking patterns, alternating bass, melody over a bass line, and arpeggios of every chord type across the neck.

lessons.title: Picking patterns: p-i-m-i, p-a-m-i and 3/4
theory: A picking pattern is a fixed order of fingers that repeats over each chord: once the right hand knows it, you only think about the chord changes.
p-i-m-i goes bass, 3rd string, 2nd string, back to the 3rd: a gentle rocking. p-a-m-i plays the bass and then rolls down from the 1st string to the 3rd.
In 3/4 a six-note pattern (p i m a m i) fills the bar: one bass note per bar, on the strong beat.
Let every note ring: keep the whole chord pressed while the fingers pick. A finger that lifts too early cuts the arpeggio short.

exercises.title: p-i-m-i over C
exercises.theory: Thumb on the root (C, 5th string), then index on G and middle on C, and back to the index. Four notes per pattern, twice.

exercises.title: p-i-m-i over Am, bass moving to E
exercises.theory: The second time the thumb plays E on the 4th string instead of A: changing the bass note inside one chord already gives movement.

exercises.title: p-a-m-i over Em
exercises.theory: The bass, then a rolling descent from the high E: ring, middle, index. Em uses many open strings, so you can focus on the right hand.

exercises.title: Waltz pattern in 3/4: Am and E
exercises.theory: p i m a m i, one bar on Am and one on E. The pattern is identical; only the thumb's string and the chord shape change.

lessons.title: Alternating bass (Travis picking)
theory: In alternating-bass picking the thumb keeps a steady pulse, jumping between two bass notes of the chord (usually the root and the 5th), while the fingers add notes in between.
Learn the thumb alone first, until it runs on its own like a bass player. Then add one finger note between thumb strokes.
The thumb plays on the beats and the fingers mostly on the offbeats, so the pattern sounds like two instruments: a bass and a little melody.
On C the thumb alternates between the 5th and 4th strings and sometimes the 6th (G, the 5th of C, with a finger moved). On G it alternates between the 6th and 4th strings.

exercises.title: The thumb alone over C
exercises.theory: C, E, G, E: root, 3rd, 5th, 3rd, steady as a clock. The thumb has to keep this going without thinking before the fingers join in.

exercises.title: Travis pattern over C
exercises.theory: Thumb, finger, thumb, finger: the bass line C-E-G-E with C and G above it. Keep the thumb exactly even; the finger notes fit in the spaces.

exercises.title: Travis pattern over G
exercises.theory: Bass between G (6th string) and D (4th string), the root and the 5th; the fingers play B, G and finally the high G.

exercises.title: Travis over Am, then D
exercises.theory: Over Am the thumb alternates A and E; over D it plays D on the 4th string. Changing chords without stopping the thumb is the real exercise.

exercises.title: Travis with a pinch
exercises.theory: A pinch is the thumb and a finger picking at the same moment: here the bass C or G with the high E on top. The listener hears both notes, so let the two ring together instead of rolling them.

lessons.title: Melody over a bass line
theory: The next step: the fingers stop playing chord notes at random and play a melody on the top strings, while the thumb keeps the bass going.
Think of two voices: the thumb is the bass player, the fingers are the singer. Each must make sense on its own.
Play the melody alone first, then the bass alone, then put them together slowly.

exercises.title: A melody in C over its bass
exercises.theory: The melody E-F-G-F-E-D-C sits on the top strings; between its notes the thumb plays C, E, G and D. The melody steps down to C just as the bass returns to C.

exercises.title: Folk study in Am: Am, Dm, E, Am
exercises.theory: One p-i-m-a sweep per chord: Am, Dm, E and back to Am. The top notes E-F-E-E and the bass A-D-E-A make two lines that move together.

exercises.title: Broken chords: C, Am, F, G with a pick or fingers
exercises.theory: Each chord played as an arpeggio from its bass upward: I-vi-IV-V in C. It's the accompaniment of countless ballads, and it works with a pick too.

lessons.title: Triad arpeggios across the neck
theory: An arpeggio plays a chord's notes one after another: for a triad, root, 3rd and 5th, repeated in higher octaves.
Movable two-octave shapes follow the barre chords: the major arpeggio with the root on the 6th string matches the E-shape barre; the minor one matches the Em shape.
Say the chord tone as you play it (1, 3, 5): knowing which note is the 3rd is what lets you aim at it in a solo.
tutorials: major minor arpeggio shapes two octaves guitar

exercises.title: A major, two octaves (root on the 6th string)
exercises.theory: A C# E across two octaves, inside the A barre (E shape at fret 5). C# is the major 3rd: four frets above the root.

exercises.title: A minor, two octaves, up and down
exercises.theory: A C E: the same shape as A major with the 3rd one fret lower. Compare both and hear how one note changes the mood.

exercises.title: C major at fret 8
exercises.theory: The A major shape moved up three frets plays C. Arpeggio shapes move like barre chords: the root decides the name.

exercises.title: G major in 2nd position
exercises.theory: G B D from the 6th string at fret 3. Low on the neck the shape changes, but the order 1-3-5 never does.

exercises.title: Which notes make the triad?
exercises.theory: Major 1-3-5, minor 1-♭3-5, diminished 1-♭3-♭5, augmented 1-3-#5: the notes you play in each arpeggio.

lessons.title: Seventh-chord arpeggios
theory: Seventh arpeggios add a fourth note: maj7 (1 3 5 7), dominant 7 (1 3 5 ♭7), minor 7 (1 ♭3 5 ♭7) and m7♭5 (1 ♭3 ♭5 ♭7).
These are the arpeggios of the chords of a key: in C, Cmaj7, Dm7, Em7, Fmaj7, G7, Am7 and Bm7♭5. Playing them is the most direct way to make a solo follow the harmony.
The 7th is the color note: a half step below the root (maj7), or a whole step below it (♭7).
tutorials: seventh chord arpeggios guitar maj7 m7 dominant

exercises.title: Cmaj7, two octaves
exercises.theory: C E G B: the major 7th (B) sits a half step below the next C. That closeness is what gives maj7 its soft, dreamy shimmer.

exercises.title: G7, two octaves, up and down
exercises.theory: G B D F: B and F form a tritone, the tension that wants to resolve to C. Hear it inside the arpeggio.

exercises.title: Am7, two octaves
exercises.theory: A C E G: a minor triad plus the ♭7. Am7 contains a C major triad (C E G) on top: relative chords share notes.

exercises.title: Bm7♭5, two octaves
exercises.theory: B D F A: the vii chord of C major. Its ♭5 (F) makes it unstable; over a G7 it sounds like G9 without the root.

exercises.title: Which notes make the seventh chord?
exercises.theory: Spell from the root with the formula, then play the notes in order: that's the arpeggio.

levels.title: The blues
levels.subtitle: Shuffle, thirds that follow the chords, bends with a target, phrases that answer, and a story in three choruses.

lessons.title: The shuffle and the 12-bar form
theory: Shuffle eighths are long-short, like the first and last notes of a triplet: "daa-da, daa-da".
Hear the form as three turns: bar 5 goes to the IV, bar 9 to the V, bar 11 back home to the I.
Quick change: bar 2 visits the IV and comes back. Both versions are real blues; the recording you play with decides.
The last bar (the V) is the turnaround: it sends you back to the top. To end the song, stay on the I.
tips: Tap your foot on 2 and 4: the backbeat is where the blues feels heavy.
Listen: Freddie King's instrumentals and Muddy Waters' Chicago band are shuffle schools in themselves.

exercises.title: Boogie bass line in A
exercises.theory: The boogie line moves between the root, 3rd, 5th, 6th and flat 7th of the chord: it spells out an A7 in the bass. Play it with a long-short shuffle feel.

exercises.title: The same line in E, on the low string
exercises.theory: The same intervals from E: the shape on the guitar is identical, just one string lower. That's the power of patterns: learn it once, play it in any key.

exercises.title: Shuffle in E, quick change
exercises.theory: The quick change visits the IV in bar 2 and comes back to the I in bar 3. Listen for it before playing: the form is the same, only that bar changes.

lessons.title: Minor third, major third
theory: The minor pentatonic has C over A7, but the chord has C#. The blues lives on that clash: C is the cry, C# the answer.
Every chord has its own pair: C→C# on A7, F→F# on D7, G→G# on E7.
Thirds and sevenths name a chord better than its root: land on one of them right when the chord changes.
In a slow minor blues the minor third is home and doesn't need to resolve (see the minor blues lesson).
tips: Hammer, slide or nudge the minor third up to the major third: don't sit on the minor third over a major chord.
Listening test: play your usual pentatonic, but stop on C#, F# and G# in bars 1, 5 and 9. The changes suddenly appear.
tutorials: blues guitar minor third to major third
mixing major and minor pentatonic blues

exercises.title: C to C# over A7
exercises.theory: C is the minor 3rd of A, C# the major 3rd. Sliding or hammering from one to the other is the most typical gesture of blues guitar.

exercises.title: F to F# over D7
exercises.theory: Over D7 the same move happens from F to F#. Every chord of the blues has its own minor-to-major third: follow the chord, not just the scale.

exercises.title: G to G# over E7
exercises.theory: Over E7 it's G to G#. Landing on G# right when the E7 arrives makes the V chord sound unmistakable.

exercises.title: Land on each chord's third: C# (A7), F# (D7), G# (E7), C# (A7)
exercises.theory: Chord tones on the change: C# for A7, F# for D7, G# for E7. Target notes like these make a solo follow the harmony instead of just floating over it.

lessons.title: Bends with a target
theory: A bend isn't "push as far as you can": it goes from one note to another, specific note.
Hear the target first: play fret 9 on the G string, then bend fret 7 until it sounds the same.
Hold it: one or two seconds right on pitch, without creeping up or sagging.
Push with two or three fingers together and turn the wrist, as if turning a key.
tips: A half-step bend on the minor third (C → C# over A) is the "curl" that sounds so bluesy.
Stop if you feel sharp pain or numbness; build strength little by little.
Listen: B.B. King and Albert King made a career out of bending to exact notes.

exercises.title: Whole-step bend: G string, fret 7 → E
exercises.theory: A whole-step bend from fret 7 on the G string reaches the pitch of fret 9 (E). Fingers 1, 2 and 3 push together; the wrist turns.

exercises.title: Whole-step bend: B string, fret 8 → A
exercises.theory: On the B string the bend goes toward the floor or the ceiling; pushing up toward the G string is the common choice. Target: the pitch of fret 10 (A).

exercises.title: Half-step curl: G string, fret 5 → C#
exercises.theory: A quarter or half bend on the minor 3rd (C) toward C# is the "curl": the blue note pushed toward the major 3rd without arriving all the way.

lessons.title: Call and response
theory: The blues talks: one phrase asks, the next one answers. The voice asks and the guitar answers, or your guitar does both.
A phrase has five parts: where it starts, its rhythm, its direction, the note it lands on and how it ends.
A good answer keeps one thing from the question (the rhythm, the direction or the last note) and changes another.
Leave space after each phrase: the silence lets the answer be heard.
Your tone lives in the attack: picking hard or soft, near the bridge or the neck, with the pick or the fingers. The same notes can sound like different players.
tips: Questions end open (on the 5th or the 4th); answers come home (to the root, or to the major third).
Listen: B.B. King's live recordings answer every vocal line with very few notes.
tutorials: call and response blues guitar lesson

exercises.title: The question: it ends open, on E
exercises.theory: A phrase that ends on the 5th (E in A) sounds open, like a question. Where a phrase ends changes its meaning more than the notes before it.

exercises.title: The answer: it comes home to A
exercises.theory: Ending on the root (A) closes the idea. The answer reuses the question's bend, so the two phrases sound related.

exercises.title: The same answer in E
exercises.theory: Moved down five frets, the same phrase answers in E. Transposing a phrase you know is the fastest way to have vocabulary in every key.

lessons.title: The turnaround
theory: Bars 11 and 12 are the turnaround: a short phrase that leads back to the top of the form.
A chromatic line falling from the 7th to the 5th (G, F#, F, E in A) is the classic way to get there.
It ends on the V chord (E7 in A): it shouldn't sound finished, it should pull you into bar 1.
tips: Play it at the end of every chorus and you'll stop losing the form.
It's the same shape in any key: move it so it starts on the root.

exercises.title: Turnaround in A
exercises.theory: The descending line G–F#–F–E moves by half steps from the flat 7 to the 5th of A, right after the high root. The chromatic motion pulls the ear toward the V.

exercises.title: The same turnaround in E
exercises.theory: The same turnaround five frets lower works in E. Learn it as a shape, then say the notes: knowing what you play makes it movable.

exercises.title: Blues in A at full speed
exercises.theory: At full speed the chart tests the form more than the fingers: know where bars 5, 9 and 11 are without counting every beat.

lessons.title: Slow minor blues: long notes
theory: In a minor blues the minor third (C in A minor) is home: it doesn't need to resolve to the major third.
Fewer notes, more weight: a slow blues exposes the bend, the vibrato and the end of every note.
Delay the vibrato: let the note sound for half a beat, then start it, keeping its center on pitch.
The E7 in bar 9 is the strongest moment: aim at G# there, the only major third in the song.
tips: Mute the string when the phrase ends: the silence keeps the pulse going.
Listen: B.B. King's "The Thrill Is Gone" is a lesson in long notes.

exercises.title: Whole-step bend: high E, fret 8 → D, held 1.5 s
exercises.theory: Holding a bend in tune for a second and a half is harder than reaching it. Listen to the pitch while it sustains and correct it with tiny wrist moves.

exercises.title: A long answer that lands on C
exercises.theory: Landing on C, the minor 3rd, sounds like home in a minor blues: it's a chord tone of Am. Add vibrato at the end so the long note stays alive.

exercises.title: Slow minor blues in A minor
exercises.theory: Slow tempos expose timing: every chord change and every rest is easy to hear. Feel the beat subdivided in three to keep the shuffle steady.

lessons.title: Eight-bar blues
theory: Not every blues has 12 bars: in the 8-bar form the V arrives as early as bar 2.
I · V · IV · IV · I · V · I-IV · I-V. Don't count it as a short 12-bar: hear its own turns.
Rhythm and lead share the same time: when you go back from a phrase to the chords, the pulse mustn't skip.
tips: Listen: "Key to the Highway" (Big Bill Broonzy, later Derek and the Dominos) is the 8-bar classic.
tutorials: key to the highway guitar lesson rhythm

exercises.title: Eight-bar blues at 80%
exercises.theory: In eight bars the chords change faster than in twelve: there's less time on each, so anticipate the next chord earlier.

exercises.title: Eight-bar blues at full speed
exercises.theory: At full speed, feel the form in two halves of four bars. The second half ends with the turnaround that takes you back to the top.

lessons.title: Blues vocabulary: licks in A
theory: A lick is a short phrase you learn as a unit, like a word. Blues players build solos by combining and varying a vocabulary of licks.
All of these live in the A minor pentatonic at fret 5, with the blue note (E♭, the ♭5) passing between D and E.
Learn each lick slowly, then play it over the 12-bar chart: start it on different beats and change its ending. A lick only becomes yours when you can bend it to the moment.
tutorials: blues licks a minor pentatonic beginner

exercises.title: The opener: bend to the fifth, land on the root
exercises.theory: D bent up to E (the 4th pushed to the 5th), then E, the high A, and down to the A on the 4th string. Starting on a bend announces the solo.

exercises.title: Climbing through the blue note
exercises.theory: D, E♭, E: the ♭5 used as a chromatic passing note on the way up. On its own E♭ sounds wrong; passing through it, it sounds like the blues.

exercises.title: Pull-off cascade down the box
exercises.theory: Two notes per string with one pick stroke each: C-A, G-E, D-C, A-G, then E and the low A. The pull-offs make the line roll downhill.

exercises.title: In the second box: bend D to E
exercises.theory: The second pentatonic box sits just above the first (frets 8 to 10). The same notes in a new place give new bends: here D up to E on the high string, ending on E with vibrato.

exercises.title: Bend, release, root, twice
exercises.theory: G bent to A and released, answered by the high A, twice. Repetition is the blues' favorite device: say it once, say it again, then go somewhere else.

lessons.title: Licks that follow the chords
theory: The pentatonic works over the whole blues, but the best licks change with the chords: they land on notes of the chord that's sounding.
Over D7 (the IV) aim for F#, its 3rd, and C, its ♭7. Over E7 (the V) aim for G#, its 3rd: it's the note that makes the V unmistakable.
Open position has its own sound: in E, the open strings ring against fretted notes, and the minor-to-major third (G to G#) is one hammer-on away.
tutorials: blues licks over the iv and v chord

exercises.title: Over D7: land on F#
exercises.theory: A, C, D, F#, A, F#: the 5th, ♭7, root and 3rd of D7. Ending on F# with vibrato tells the ear the harmony moved to the IV.

exercises.title: Over E7: the G# line
exercises.theory: E, G#, B, G#, D, G#: an E7 arpeggio that keeps returning to G#. That note isn't in the A minor pentatonic, which is exactly why it stands out on the V.

exercises.title: A rising turnaround
exercises.theory: A, then E rising by half steps to G, and down to E: the climb from the 5th to the ♭7 builds tension and lands on the V, ready for the top of the form.

exercises.title: Open E: minor to major third
exercises.theory: E, then G hammered to G#, A, B, and the G-G# hammer again, ending on the low E. The open G string makes the minor third; one fret up is the major third.

exercises.title: Open E: low riff with the blue note
exercises.theory: E, G, A, B♭, B, then the E an octave up and back down. B♭ is the ♭5 of E: in the low register it growls.

exercises.title: Double stops in A
exercises.theory: Two strings picked together: D and G lean on the IV sound, then C and E (the minor 3rd and the 5th of A) pull back home. Mute the strings around them with the fretting hand so only the pair sounds.

lessons.title: Three choruses, one story
theory: Chorus 1 states a motif, low and with few notes. Chorus 2 repeats it with a change. Chorus 3 goes higher or louder, then ends clearly.
Develop it by changing one thing at a time: the ending, the register, the rhythm or the dynamics. Change everything and nobody recognizes the motif.
More and faster isn't the only way to build: space, repetition and register build too.

Turn a scale into music: add rests, repeat a rhythm, and hold the notes that belong to the chord. A scale played note after note sounds like an exercise; the same notes with space and repetition sound like a phrase.
tips: Record the three choruses without stopping. If you make a mistake, keep going: that's practice too.
tutorials: how to build a blues solo three choruses

exercises.title: The motif
exercises.theory: A motif is a short idea that can be repeated and changed. Six notes are enough: the shorter the motif, the easier it is to recognize when it comes back.

exercises.title: The same motif, a new ending
exercises.theory: Same beginning, new ending: the listener recognizes the motif and enjoys the surprise. Change one thing, keep the rest.

exercises.title: The motif an octave up
exercises.theory: Moving a motif up an octave raises the energy without new notes. Register is one of the simplest ways to build a solo.

exercises.title: Three choruses in A, with an ending
exercises.theory: Three choruses: present the idea, develop it, peak and close. Plan the ending before you start: a clear last note makes the whole solo sound intentional.

levels.title: Songs
levels.subtitle: Real songs: their chords, their form, the techniques they use, and the chart at your own pace.

lessons.title: November Rain (Guns N' Roses)
theory: The record is tuned a half step down and sounds in B major. In standard tuning you play the same shapes in C: F, Dm, C and G.
The verse walks F → Dm → C: two chords that share notes (F and A) and then a rest on C, the home chord.
The chorus swaps the start: Dm → G → C. G pulls back to C, so every line closes at home.
It's a slow ballad: every chord lasts a full bar. Your job is to change on time and let each one ring.
tips: The F barre is the hard part. If it doesn't ring yet, play the small F (strings 1 to 4) and move to the full barre later.
Change during the last beat of the bar, not after the first beat of the next one.
Strum softly: one long down strum on beat 1, and a light down-down-up at the end of the bar.
Play along with the record only after you retune a half step down; for grading here, stay in standard tuning.

exercises.title: Ring the F barre four times
exercises.theory: The F barre needs every string clean. Check them one by one, slowly; the strings that don't ring tell you which finger to adjust.

exercises.title: F ↔ Dm (verse)
exercises.theory: F and Dm share F and A: Dm is the relative minor of F. Two chords with the same notes but a different bass sound close yet different in mood.

exercises.title: Dm → G → C (chorus)
exercises.theory: ii–V–I in C: Dm prepares, G pulls, C resolves. The most common cadence in Western music, here in a rock ballad.

exercises.title: Ballad bend: G string, fret 7 → E
exercises.theory: In a ballad a bend is a sung note: slow, in tune and held. Reach the target pitch, then let it ring before adding vibrato.

exercises.title: A slow phrase in C, ending with vibrato
exercises.theory: This phrase uses the C major pentatonic and ends with vibrato. Phrasing (where you breathe, what you hold) matters more than the number of notes.

exercises.title: The whole chart at 70%
exercises.theory: At 70% you have time to listen to each chord ring. Use it to make every change land exactly on beat 1.

exercises.title: The whole chart at full speed
exercises.theory: At full speed the slow ballad still asks for patience: one chord per bar, let it breathe, don't rush the changes.

lessons.title: Comfortably Numb (Pink Floyd)
theory: Standard tuning. The verse is in B minor: Bm → A → G → Em, and back to Bm.
The chorus moves to D major, the relative major of B minor: same notes, a brighter home.
In the chorus, C is borrowed (it isn't in D major): it gives that floating feel before G and A take you back.
The famous solos live in the B minor pentatonic around fret 7 and 10: long bends, wide vibrato and lots of space.
tips: Bm is a barre at fret 2. If it doesn't ring yet, play only strings 1 to 4.
It's slow (about 64 BPM): count four beats per chord out loud before you play along.
In a bend, the target pitch matters more than the speed: go up slowly until it sounds right, then hold it.
Leave silence between phrases. In this style, the space is part of the solo.
tutorials: how to bend in tune guitar

exercises.title: Bm ↔ A (verse)
exercises.theory: Bm to A is i to VII in B minor: a whole step down. That step is one of the most typical moves of rock in minor keys.

exercises.title: G ↔ Em (verse)
exercises.theory: G and Em are VI and iv in B minor. Em shares two notes with G (G and B): that's why the change feels so smooth.

exercises.title: D → A → C → G (chorus)
exercises.theory: In D major, C is the borrowed flat VII: a whole step below the I. It adds a floating, open color before the progression comes home.

exercises.title: Long bend: B string, fret 10 → B
exercises.theory: A long bend held for two seconds: listen to the pitch the whole time. A slow, wide vibrato at the end is the signature of this style.

exercises.title: B minor pentatonic at fret 7, down and up
exercises.theory: B minor pentatonic at fret 7 is the same box as A minor at fret 5, two frets higher. One shape, any key: just move the root.

exercises.title: Bend, release and answer with vibrato
exercises.theory: Bend, release, then answer: a bend up and back down is a complete gesture. Make the release in time, as if it were a written note.

exercises.title: The whole chart at 70%
exercises.theory: The verse is in B minor and the chorus in D major, its relative major. Notice how the same notes feel darker or brighter depending on the home chord.

exercises.title: The whole chart at full speed
exercises.theory: At full speed, keep the strumming relaxed and the changes on time: the song's power comes from steadiness, not from force.

levels.title: Reading the neck
levels.subtitle: Half steps, intervals by ear and by fret, finding notes and thinking in degrees.

lessons.title: Sharps, flats and half steps
theory: On a piano, going from one key to the very next one (white or black) is a half step. On a guitar, one fret is a half step.
There's a black key between most natural notes. Only E–F and B–C are a half step apart, with nothing in between.
A black key has two names: C♯ (C raised) is the same pitch as D♭ (D lowered). Which name you use depends on the key you're in.
Two frets make a whole step: C to D, E to F♯, B to C♯.
tips: Play a natural note, then the same note one fret higher, and name both ways: F, F♯ = G♭.
tutorials: half steps and whole steps guitar
captions: One octave of a piano: tap a key to hear it. Black keys carry both names.
The natural notes on the 6th and 5th strings. The empty frets between them are the sharps and flats.

exercises.title: Half steps, whole steps and two names
exercises.theory: A half step is the smallest distance in Western music: one fret. Two half steps make a whole step. E–F and B–C are natural half steps, with no note between them.

exercises.title: Find the natural notes on the neck
exercises.theory: Natural notes on one string are two frets apart, except E–F and B–C, which are one fret apart. Start from the open string's name and walk up.

exercises.title: Play the note on the string
exercises.theory: Knowing a note's name and playing it are different skills. Here you go from the name to the fret: the reverse of reading tab.

lessons.title: Intervals: counting frets
theory: An interval is the distance between two notes, counted in half steps, which on the guitar means frets.
The ones you'll use most: minor 3rd = 3 frets, major 3rd = 4, perfect 4th = 5, perfect 5th = 7, octave = 12.
Across strings the count still works: the next string up starts 5 frets higher (4 between the G and B strings).
Every interval has its own sound: the major 3rd is bright, the minor 3rd darker, the 5th open and hollow.
tips: Hum the two notes after you play them. Linking the sound to the shape is what makes intervals stick.
captions: A major on one string, labeled by degree. The distance from 1 to each number is an interval.

exercises.title: Name the interval by its frets
exercises.theory: Count the half steps between the two notes: 3 is a minor 3rd, 4 a major 3rd, 5 a perfect 4th, 7 a perfect 5th, 12 an octave.

exercises.title: Play a 3rd, a 5th or an octave
exercises.theory: The 3rd, 5th and octave are the skeleton of every major chord. On adjacent strings: the 5th is one string up and two frets up; the octave, two strings up and two frets up.

exercises.title: Play a minor 3rd, a 4th or a 6th
exercises.theory: The minor 3rd (3 frets) makes a chord minor; the 4th (5 frets) is the distance between most open strings; the major 6th (9 frets) is the minor 3rd turned upside down.

lessons.title: Hearing intervals
theory: Ear training links a sound to a name. Start with a few intervals that sound very different, then add the closer ones.
Sing the two notes back after you hear them. If you can sing it, you can find it on the neck.
Naming what you hear and playing it are two different skills, so they're two separate exercises here.
tips: Don't guess fast: replay the pair, sing it, and compare it with intervals you already know.
tutorials: how to recognize intervals by ear

exercises.title: Third, fifth or octave?
exercises.theory: The octave sounds like the same note, higher. The 5th sounds hollow and stable. The major 3rd sounds bright and sweet. Start by telling these three apart.

exercises.title: Thirds, fourths and fifths
exercises.theory: Thirds sound like a chord; the 4th sounds open and slightly unresolved, as if it wanted to fall to the 3rd; the 5th sounds stable. Sing them to feel the difference.

exercises.title: Now play them
exercises.theory: Hearing an interval and finding it on the neck links the ear to the hand. Sing the target note before you play it.

exercises.title: Echo a short phrase
exercises.theory: Echoing a phrase is how musicians learn by ear: listen, sing, then find. Keep it short, and find the first note before worrying about the rest.

lessons.title: Find the note
theory: Learn the natural notes on the 6th and 5th strings first: they're where the roots of most chord shapes live.
Use the fret markers as landmarks. On the 6th string, frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 are G, A, B, C♯ and E.
The octave shape finds the same note higher up: two strings up and two frets up (three frets when you cross the B string).
tips: Practice in short bursts: five notes, then rest. Accuracy first, speed later.
tutorials: learn the notes on the guitar neck
captions: Natural notes on the 6th and 5th strings.

exercises.title: Mark every one on the low strings
exercises.theory: The notes of the 6th and 5th strings are the roots of most barre chords and power chords. Mark them all and look for landmarks like the 5th, 7th and 12th frets.

exercises.title: On the 6th string
exercises.theory: On the 6th string: F at 1, G at 3, A at 5, B at 7, C at 8, D at 10, E at 12. Learn these seven and the sharps and flats are the frets in between.

exercises.title: On the 5th string
exercises.theory: On the 5th string: B at 2, C at 3, D at 5, E at 7, F at 8, G at 10, A at 12. It's the 6th string's map moved five frets.

exercises.title: 6th, 5th and 4th strings
exercises.theory: The 4th string is the 5th string's pattern five frets further, just as the 5th was the 6th's. Use what you know from the string below.

lessons.title: Name the marked note
theory: The musical alphabet has seven letters: A B C D E F G, and then A again. On one string each fret is a half step, so the natural notes are two frets apart, except E–F and B–C, which are one fret apart.
Learn the low two strings first: that's where the roots of almost every chord shape live. Name each note out loud as you find it.
A quick method: memorize the notes at frets 5, 7 and 12 on every string, then count a fret or two from there.
tips: Use the fret markers as landmarks: on the 6th string, frets 3, 5, 7 and 9 are G, A, B and C♯.
tutorials: memorize notes on the guitar fretboard
captions: The natural notes on the 6th and 5th strings.

exercises.title: Name it on the low strings
exercises.theory: Name each marked note by counting from the nearest landmark you know, not from the open string every time.

exercises.title: Name it anywhere, sharps and flats too
exercises.theory: A fret between two naturals has two names: the lower note sharp or the upper note flat. Either is correct here; in a key, only one is.

lessons.title: Fret 12: the neck starts over
theory: At the 12th fret every string sounds its open note an octave higher. From there up, the neck repeats: fret 13 is fret 1 again, fret 15 is fret 3, and so on.
That's why the double dot sits at the 12th fret: it's the halfway point of the string.
Natural harmonics at fret 12 sound the same octave: touch the string lightly right over the fret wire and pick.
tips: To find a note above the 12th fret, find it below and add 12.

exercises.title: Name the notes at frets 0 and 12
exercises.theory: Fret 12 divides the string in half, so it sounds exactly one octave above the open string: same name, double frequency.

exercises.title: Name it between frets 12 and 17
exercises.theory: Above fret 12 subtract 12 and use the map you already know: fret 15 is fret 3, fret 17 is fret 5.

lessons.title: Octaves: the shortcut
theory: The same note shows up all over the neck in octaves, always in the same shapes. From a note on the 6th or 5th string: two strings up and two frets up. From the 4th or 3rd string: two strings up and three frets up (the B string is tuned one fret lower).
Knowing one note and its octave shapes is enough to find it everywhere.
Octaves are also a sound: playing the same melody in two octaves at once thickens it, a classic in jazz and rock.
tips: Play the two notes of an octave together, muting the string in between: that's the octave sound of so much jazz and funk.
captions: The notes of G major pentatonic: find each G and its octaves.

exercises.title: Click every octave of the note
exercises.theory: One note, many places: octave shapes connect them. From any note you can jump two strings and two frets, or two strings and three frets past the B string.

lessons.title: Degrees: a map that moves with the key
theory: A degree names a note by its place in the key: 1 is the root, 3 the third, 5 the fifth. In G the 3rd is B; in A it's C♯.
Degree shapes don't change when the key does: move the root and every degree moves with it.
Learn where 1, 3 and 5 sit around a root. That's every major chord, in every key.
tips: Say degrees, not letters, while you practice a shape: “1, 3, 5” works in any key.
captions: G major around fret 2, labeled by degree. Move it up two frets and it's A major.

exercises.title: Find every root
exercises.theory: The root (1) is the note that names the key or chord. Find every root first; every other degree is measured from it.

exercises.title: Find every 3rd
exercises.theory: The major 3rd is four frets above the root on the same string, or one string up and one fret back. It's the note that makes a chord major.

exercises.title: Which note is that degree?
exercises.theory: A degree is a position in the scale: in D major, 3 is F# and 5 is A. Thinking in degrees lets you move any idea to any key.

levels.title: Reading rhythm II
levels.subtitle: Sixteenths, dotted notes, triplets, syncopation and dictation.

lessons.title: Sixteenth notes
theory: A sixteenth note is a quarter of a beat: four of them fit in every click. It's written with two beams (or two flags). Count "1 e and a" quietly, without speeding up.
Pick sixteenths with strict alternate picking: down on "1" and "and", up on "e" and "a". The hand never changes its rhythm.
tips: Pick down-up-down-up, one stroke per sixteenth. The hand keeps moving even when it doesn't play.

figures.pattern: s s s s q q q
e s s q e s s q

captions: One beat of sixteenths and three quarters.
An eighth and two sixteenths: the rock gallop.

exercises.title: Tap the sixteenths
patterns: q s s s s q q

s s e s s e q q
q q s s s s q
exercises.theory: Four sixteenths fill one beat. Keep them even: the most common mistake is to rush the middle two.

lessons.title: The dotted eighth
theory: A dot next to a note adds half its value. A dotted eighth lasts ¾ of a beat, and it almost always comes with a sixteenth that completes the beat: the limping feel of many riffs.
The dotted-eighth-plus-sixteenth figure gives the bouncing, limping feel of many rock and blues riffs.
tips: Think in sixteenths: the dotted eighth lasts three of them, the sixteenth one. "1 – – a 2 – – a".

figures.pattern: e. s e. s q q

captions: Two dotted eighths with sixteenths, then two quarters.

exercises.theory: A dotted eighth plus a sixteenth fill one beat: long (three quarters) and short (one quarter). Count "1 e and a" and play on "1" and "a".

lessons.title: Triplets
theory: A triplet splits the beat in three equal parts instead of two or four. It's written with a 3 over the group. Count "trip-o-let" or "1-2-3" inside every click.
A shuffle is a triplet with the first two notes tied: long-short. Practice straight triplets first, then tie them.
tips: Lots of blues and 12/8 ballads live on triplets. The shuffle is a triplet with the middle note left out.

figures.pattern: te te te q te te te q

captions: Eighth-note triplets alternating with quarters.

q q te te te q

exercises.theory: Three equal notes in one beat: they sound rounder than eighths. Say "tri-po-let" without stretching the first syllable.

lessons.title: Syncopation
theory: Syncopation is when a note starts on a weak spot (on the "and") and holds over the next strong beat. That's the push that makes funk and so much else move forward.
Syncopation only works if the pulse is clear. Tap the beat with your foot while your hands play off it.
tips: Tap your foot on every beat and play only where it's written. The foot doesn't follow the hand.
captions: Eighth, a quarter on the off-beat, eighth: the attack lands on the "and" of 1.
Dotted quarter: the second attack lands on the "and" of 2.

exercises.title: Tap the syncopations

exercises.theory: A syncopated note starts on a weak part of the beat and lasts through the next strong one. Keep counting the beat underneath: that's what makes the push felt.

lessons.title: Dictation I
theory: In a dictation it goes the other way: the app plays a bar and you choose the notation. It's what happens when you figure out a song by ear.
Write what you hear one beat at a time. Most bars are made of a few common groups: one quarter, two eighths, four sixteenths, an eighth and two sixteenths.
tips: Listen once all the way through, then again paying attention to one beat at a time.

exercises.theory: Listen once for the beat, then once for the rhythm inside it. Match the groups of each beat before looking at the whole bar.

lessons.title: Dictation II
theory: Now with the new values. A triplet sounds round, rolling; a dotted eighth sounds like it limps; a syncopation sounds early, ahead of the beat.
If a beat sounds uneven, ask: is it long-short (dotted) or three equal notes (triplet)?

lessons.title: Rhythm II on the guitar
theory: Close the level playing for real: the open low E string, the new rhythms, and the listener measuring every attack in milliseconds.
Use a metronome at a tempo where everything is clean, then speed up in small steps.
tips: If your notes always come out early or late, run guitarr calibrate once.

exercises.theory: Fast values need a small, relaxed picking motion. Alternate picking keeps sixteenths even: down on the beat and the "and", up in between.

levels.title: Reading notation
levels.subtitle: From tab to the staff: the treble clef, position by position.

lessons.title: The staff and the clef
theory: The staff has five lines and four spaces: the higher a note sits, the higher it sounds. The clef at the start says which note lives on which line.
Guitar is written in the treble clef, an octave above how it sounds, so its notes fit on the staff. That's why the clef has a small 8 under it.
tips: Notes beyond the staff get ledger lines: short lines that carry the staff up or down.
tutorials: how to read treble clef guitar
captions: The open strings on the staff, from the lowest to the highest.

exercises.title: How the staff works
exercises.theory: The staff measures pitch vertically: each line and space is one letter. The treble clef curls around the second line from the bottom, which is G.

lessons.title: Open strings on the staff
theory: Start with the open strings: they're the landmarks for everything else. Notice where each one sits, on a line or in a space, and how many ledger lines it needs.
Guitar music sounds an octave lower than written: the written E on the top space is the open 1st string.
captions: Open strings, from the lowest to the highest.

exercises.title: Name the open string
exercises.theory: The low E sits three ledger lines below the staff; the high E on the top space. The four strings in between climb through the lines and spaces.

lessons.title: Natural notes on the low strings
theory: Now the natural notes (no sharps or flats) of the two lowest strings, up to the 5th fret. Each letter of the musical alphabet moves the note one step on the staff, from a line to a space or the other way round.
Ledger lines extend the staff below and above it. The low E string needs three ledger lines; the A string, two.
captions: Naturals on the 6th string: E, F, G, A.
Naturals on the 5th string: A, B, C, D.

exercises.title: Name the note
exercises.theory: Each step up the musical alphabet moves the note from a line to the next space, or from a space to the next line.

lessons.title: Natural notes on every string
theory: With every string, the first position covers more than two octaves. Use the open strings as anchors: find the nearest open string and count steps from it.
Group the notes you know by string: E string F G, B string C D, and so on. Two or three notes per string cover all of first position.

exercises.title: Name the note in first position
exercises.theory: Use the open strings as anchors: E, A, D, G, B, E. A fretted note in first position is never more than four frets from one of them.

lessons.title: From the staff to the neck
theory: Reading means knowing where to play. The app shows a note on the staff and you click it on the neck at the exact height: the same note an octave up or down doesn't count.
In first position each fret is played by the finger with its number: fret 1 by finger 1, fret 2 by finger 2, and so on.
tips: Some notes exist on two strings (the 5th fret of one string = the next open string). Both count: it's the same pitch.

exercises.title: Click the written note
exercises.theory: A written note has one exact pitch, but on the guitar it may live on two or three strings. In first position choose the lowest fret available.

lessons.title: Sharps and flats on the staff
theory: A sharp (♯) before a note raises it a half step; a flat (♭) lowers it a half step. On the staff the note stays in the same place and just gets the sign in front. On the neck it's the next fret.
Key signatures put the sharps or flats at the start of each line, so you don't have to write them on every note.
captions: F, F♯, G, G♯ on the 6th string.
The same frets spelled with flats: F, G♭, G, A♭.

exercises.title: Name the note, sharps and flats too
exercises.theory: An accidental lasts until the end of the bar. A natural sign (♮) cancels it.

lessons.title: Reading in 5th position
theory: Readers don't stay stuck in first position. In 5th position, finger 1 sits on fret 5 and each finger takes care of one fret (5 to 8). The notes on the staff are the same; only where they live on the neck changes.
Positions are named after the fret under finger 1. Knowing several positions lets you play a melody where it sounds and fits best.
tips: Use the string above as a shortcut: the 5th fret of one string is the next open string (except G→B, which is the 4th fret).
captions: On the 6th string, frets 5, 7 and 8: A, B, C.

exercises.title: Click it in 5th position
exercises.theory: In 5th position each finger owns a fret: 1 on fret 5, 2 on 6, 3 on 7, 4 on 8. The hand stays still and only the fingers move.

lessons.title: Reading in 7th position
theory: In 7th position (frets 7 to 10), many notes that were open strings in first position become fretted. It's a great position to read scales in sharp keys such as D and A major.
When reading in a new position, say the note and the finger out loud for the first few bars.
tips: Choose a position before you start reading and stay in it: a still hand makes every note easier to find.

exercises.title: Read and play in 7th position
exercises.theory: 7th position covers frets 7 to 10. Many keys with sharps fit well here, so it's a favorite spot for reading melodies.

lessons.title: Reading on the guitar
theory: The finish: the note shows up on the staff and you play it on the guitar. It's the first step to reading real notation note by note, the way you read tab.
Read slowly but without stopping: a steady pulse with a few wrong notes trains reading better than a perfect stop-and-go.
tips: Play it at the written height: the listener wants that exact note, not the same name an octave away.

exercises.title: Read and play in first position
exercises.theory: Read, find, play: say the note name, picture its place on the neck, then play it. Speed comes from repetition, not from guessing.

levels.title: Scales
levels.subtitle: Build scales from their steps, spell them in every key, and play them across the neck.

lessons.title: Building the major scale
theory: The major scale is a pattern of steps: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half (W W H W W W H).
Start on any note and follow the pattern. From C you get C D E F G A B C, with no sharps or flats.
Each note is a degree, 1 to 7. The half steps always fall between 3–4 and 7–1.
tips: Play it on one string first: you'll see the steps as fret distances (2 2 1 2 2 2 1).
tutorials: how to build the major scale
captions: C major on one string: the frets between neighbors go 2 2 1 2 2 2 1.

exercises.title: C major on one string
exercises.theory: On one string the step pattern is visible: two frets for a whole step, one for a half. From C on the 5th string: 2-2-1-2-2-2-1 frets.

exercises.title: G major in one position
exercises.theory: In one position the same scale fits under the hand across all six strings. Fingers 1 to 4 each take a fret; the stretches come from the half steps.

exercises.title: Degrees of the major scale
exercises.theory: Degrees are counted from the key's root: in G major, 4 is C and 7 is F#. The 3rd and 7th are the notes that change most between scales.

lessons.title: The major scale in all 12 keys
theory: A major scale uses each letter from A to G exactly once. So F♯ major has E♯, not F, and G♭ major has C♭, not B.
Keys with sharps go up in fifths: G (1♯), D (2), A (3), E (4), B (5), F♯ (6).
Keys with flats go the other way: F (1♭), B♭ (2), E♭ (3), A♭ (4), D♭ (5), G♭ (6).
The shape on the guitar doesn't care about names: the same fingering works in every key. Spelling matters when you read, write and talk about music.
To find a sharp key from its signature: the last sharp is the 7th degree, so go up a half step. For flat keys, the second-to-last flat names the key (F major has a single flat, B♭).
tips: Write a scale's letters first (one of each), then add the sharps or flats the pattern needs.

exercises.title: Spell the scale correctly
exercises.theory: Every letter appears once in a major scale. To find a key's sharps, use the order F C G D A E B; flats go the other way: B E A D G C F.

exercises.title: A major
exercises.theory: A major has three sharps: F#, C# and G#. On the guitar the pattern is the same as G major, two frets higher.

exercises.title: E♭ major
exercises.theory: E♭ major has three flats: B♭, E♭ and A♭. The fingering pattern is the same as any other major scale; find the root E♭ first and build from it.

lessons.title: Key signatures
theory: A key signature is the set of sharps or flats a key uses, written once at the start of each line instead of before every note.
Sharps are always added in the same order: F C G D A E B. Flats go the opposite way: B E A D G C F.

Reading a sharp signature: the last sharp is the 7th degree, so the key is a half step above it (three sharps, last one G#: A major). Reading a flat signature: the second-to-last flat names the key (three flats: E♭ major). One flat alone is F major.
Each signature is shared by a major key and its relative minor: three sharps is A major or F# minor. The song's home chord tells you which.
tutorials: key signatures explained circle of fifths guitar

exercises.title: How many sharps or flats?
exercises.theory: Moving a fifth up adds one sharp (C, G, D, A…); moving a fifth down adds one flat (C, F, B♭, E♭…). That chain is the circle of fifths.

exercises.title: D major (two sharps)
exercises.theory: D major has F# and C#, the first two sharps in the order. Say each sharp out loud as you play it.

exercises.title: F major (one flat)
exercises.theory: F major has a single flat, B♭: the 4th degree. Without it, the scale would sound like F Lydian.

lessons.title: Natural minor and the relative minor
theory: The natural minor scale is the major scale started on its 6th degree: A minor has the same notes as C major.
Same notes, different home. A minor sounds sad or serious because everything comes back to A.
From its own root the formula is 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7.
Every major key has a relative minor a minor 3rd below its root: G → E minor, F → D minor.
tips: Play C major, then the same notes starting and ending on A. Listen to how the home changes.
captions: A natural minor around fret 5, labeled by degree.

exercises.title: Relative minor and major
exercises.theory: The relative minor starts on the 6th degree of the major scale, three frets below its root. Same key signature, different home.

exercises.title: Major or minor? (by ear)
exercises.theory: Major scales have a major 3rd (bright); minor scales have a minor 3rd (dark). Listen to the third note: it decides the mood.

exercises.title: A natural minor
exercises.theory: A natural minor uses only white-key notes, like C major, but it starts and ends on A. Lean on A, C and E: the notes of the Am chord.

lessons.title: Major scale positions across the neck
theory: One position covers four or five frets, one finger per fret. Five positions connect to cover the whole neck.
