exercises.theory: D bent up to E, then E, G, A at the top and back down to the root on the D string.

exercises.title: A repeating triplet lick
exercises.theory: C A G three times on the top two strings, then down to D. Keep the three-note group even and let it roll.

exercises.title: Whole-step bend: G string, fret 7 → E
exercises.theory: Check the target first: fret 9 on the same string. Bend with three fingers and the wrist, not with one finger.

optional.title: Rock solos and songs
optional.subtitle: Phrasing a solo, double stops and a full rock song.

lessons.title: Phrasing a solo: call and response
theory: A good solo talks: a short phrase asks a question, the next one answers it. Leave a breath between them.
The call usually ends on an unstable note (the bend to the 5th); the answer comes home to the root.
Fewer notes, more intention: one well-placed bend with vibrato says more than a fast scale.
tutorials: rock solo phrasing call and response

exercises.title: The call
exercises.theory: A, G, E, then the bend to E on the G string: the phrase stays up in the air.

exercises.title: The answer
exercises.theory: D, C, A, G and home to A with vibrato: the question resolved.

lessons.title: Double stops
theory: A double stop is two notes played together, usually on adjacent strings. On the top two strings at the same fret they form a fourth: the rock'n'roll lead sound.
Barre the two strings with one finger and pick both at once; slide into them from a fret below for extra attitude.
Double stops sit between a riff and a solo: perfect for fills between sung lines.
tutorials: rock and roll double stops lead guitar

exercises.title: Double stops in A
exercises.theory: E with A at fret 5, G with C at fret 8 and back, then D with G and C with E on the G and B strings: two strings picked together on every note.

lessons.title: A full rock song
theory: A rock song is built from a few parts: intro riff, verse, chorus, a solo section and an ending. The riff often returns between them.
The chorus usually opens up: chords that ring after palm-muted verses, so the song gets bigger without playing faster.
Learn the form first: how many times each part repeats and what comes next. Then lock in with the drums (or the metronome).

exercises.title: The whole song at 70%
exercises.theory: Five sections in A. Watch the section names: the verse is muted, the chorus rings, the solo section repeats the riff for you to improvise over.

exercises.title: At full speed
exercises.theory: At tempo, groove first: steady eighths in the right hand, and let the accents come from the riff.

optional.title: Tango rhythm
optional.subtitle: The marcato, the síncopa and the minor-key harmony of tango.

lessons.title: Marcato in four
theory: The marcato is tango's basic accompaniment: four firm, short chords per bar, with a little more weight on beats 1 and 3.
Short means muted: release the fretting hand pressure right after each stroke so the chord stops. That dry sound is the tango bandoneón section on a guitar.
The arrastre is a drag into the beat: a quick slide or strum that starts just before the beat and lands on it, like the bandoneón's growl.

exercises.title: Marcato on the low A
patterns: q q q q
q rq q rq
q q q q
h q q
exercises.theory: Four short notes per bar. The rests in some bars are where you stop the string; the last bar is the marcato with a held 1.

exercises.title: Tango technique
exercises.theory: Marcato, síncopa, milonga, arrastre and the dominant: the vocabulary of tango guitar.

lessons.title: The síncopa
theory: The síncopa is tango's signature accent: beat 1, then an accent on the "and" of 2 that anticipates beat 3, which stays silent.
It feels like a stumble on purpose: the music leans forward and then breathes.
Alternate bars of marcato and síncopa and you have the heartbeat of a tango orchestra.

exercises.title: Tap the síncopa
patterns: q. e rq q
q q q q
q. e rq q
q. e q q
exercises.theory: A dotted quarter, an eighth, a rest and a quarter: 1, the "and" of 2, silence on 3, then 4.

lessons.title: Minor-key harmony: i – iv – V7
theory: Most tangos are in a minor key. In A minor the three chords that do the work are Am (i), Dm (iv) and E7 (V7).
E7 has G♯, a half step below A: that's why it pulls so hard back to Am. Tango loves to stretch that tension before resolving.
A7 often appears before Dm: a secondary dominant that leads into the iv chord.

exercises.title: Am → Dm → E7 → Am
exercises.theory: Keep the fingers close to the strings: Am and E7 share the shape, just one string apart.

exercises.title: A tango in A minor
exercises.theory: Marcato on every bar. A7 leads into Dm; E7 waits two bars before coming home to Am.

optional.title: Milonga and the bass
optional.subtitle: The milonga rhythm, bass lines and the bordoneo.

lessons.title: The milonga: 3 + 3 + 2
theory: The milonga is tango's faster, happier cousin. Its rhythm groups the eighths of a bar 3 + 3 + 2.
Played slow and with the thumb on the bass strings it becomes the milonga campera, the guitar music of the countryside.
Feel the last group as a spring: two short eighths that throw you into the next bar.

exercises.title: Tap the milonga
patterns: q. q. q
e. e. e e. e. e
q. q. q
e. e. e q q
exercises.theory: The 3 + 3 + 2 in full bars and in halves: dotted quarter, dotted quarter, quarter; or dotted eighths when it's twice as fast.

exercises.title: A milonga
exercises.theory: The strum is the 3 + 3 + 2: down on 1, on the "and" of 2 and on 4. A major key this time: milongas are often brighter.

lessons.title: Bass lines
theory: Tango bass lines walk: they connect chords with steps and chromatic notes instead of jumping from root to root.
In A minor, the bass going down A – G – F – E is the same line as the Andalusian cadence: tango and flamenco share it.
Play the bass with the thumb, short and firm, as if it were the double bass of the orchestra.

exercises.title: The walking bass down and back
exercises.theory: A, G, F, E and back up through F and G to A, then B: a line, not four roots.

exercises.title: A chromatic approach to Dm
exercises.theory: A, B, C, C♯ and D: the chromatic step C♯–D leads into the iv chord the way a bandoneón would.

lessons.title: Bordoneo: bass melody and arpeggio
theory: Bordoneo is the guitarist's tango and milonga accompaniment: the thumb plays a melody on the bass strings (bordones) while the fingers answer with the chord.
Keep the 3 + 3 + 2 in the thumb; the fingers fill the gaps.
Let the bass notes ring into each other only when they belong to the same chord.

exercises.title: Bordoneo on Am
exercises.theory: Bass A, then the chord tones E, A, C; bass E, then the chord again. The thumb leads, the fingers answer.

exercises.title: Bordoneo on E7, back to Am
exercises.theory: E7 spelled from the bass: E, B, D, G♯, B, then A minor: the dominant resolving in one line.

optional.title: Tango melody and a full tango
optional.subtitle: Harmonic minor melodies, the dominant and a whole tango.

lessons.title: Harmonic minor: the tango melody
theory: Tango melodies love harmonic minor: the raised 7th (G♯ in A minor) gives the line its drama and its pull to the root.
Play melodies legato and expressive, as a violin or a singer would: slide into important notes and hold them.
The F–G♯ step, three frets wide, is the sound of the old tango's lament.

exercises.title: A harmonic minor at fret 5
exercises.theory: G♯ sits on fret 6 of the D string and fret 4 of the high E: right below each A.

exercises.title: A tango melody, descending
exercises.theory: A G♯ F E D C B A, then G♯ and home: the whole harmonic minor in one sigh.

lessons.title: The dominant: tension and release
theory: E7 in A minor holds the music's breath: G♯ wants to rise to A, D wants to fall to C.
Tango often stops on the dominant, a fermata full of drama, before the last chord: the famous "chan-chan" ending is V7 then i, short and dry.
Hear the difference between a dominant seventh and a plain minor chord: the tritone inside E7 (G♯–D) is what creates the tension.

exercises.title: Dominant seventh or minor?
exercises.theory: The dominant seventh sounds like a question that needs an answer; the minor triad sounds sad but settled.

exercises.title: Endings: chan-chan
exercises.theory: Phrases of four bars, each ending on E7 → Am. Stop the last Am dead: that's the chan-chan.

lessons.title: A full tango
theory: A tango has two or three parts: a rhythmic A part in minor, a more lyrical B part (often in the relative major) and a return to A.
Change the accompaniment with the part: marcato and síncopa in A, a softer arpeggio in B.
Dynamics are everything in tango: sudden silences, a crescendo into the dominant and the chan-chan to finish.

exercises.title: The whole tango at 70%
exercises.theory: A in A minor, B in C major, A again and the ending. Watch the section names and change the feel with them.

exercises.title: At full speed
exercises.theory: At tempo, keep the marcato short and the síncopa sharp: tango is danced, and dancers need a clear beat.
